question: What do we call the natural home where germs live, grow, and multiply?
explanation: Think of a reservoir as a cozy home base where a pathogen hangs out, grows, and multiplies before it decides to move on to a new host! [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why do all the links in the chain of infection need to stay connected?

options.A: To prevent the host from developing any natural immunity
options.B: To allow the disease to successfully spread to a new host
options.C: To speed up the recovery process of the infected patient
options.D: To ensure the pathogen can multiply inside the environment

explanation: For an infection to happen, the chain must be complete from start to finish. Break any link, and you stop the spread! You've got this. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h1)

question: What do we call a healthy person who has a germ in their body without feeling sick?
explanation: Carriers look and feel totally fine, but they carry germs around and can pass them on to others without even knowing it! [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h2)

question: Dirty, contaminated drinking water plays what main role in spreading diseases?

options.A: Serving as a direct vector for viruses
options.B: Functioning as a primary portal of entry
options.D: Acting as a fully susceptible human host

explanation: Non-living things like water, food, and soil can hold onto germs and act as an environmental home base, or reservoir, for waterborne sicknesses. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is the name for a non-living object—like a table or a thermometer—that passes germs from one person to another?
explanation: Fomites are just everyday objects (like door handles or stethoscope chests) that pick up germs and share them with the next person who touches them. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h3)

question: A patient gets malaria after a mosquito bite. What type of disease spread is this?
explanation: Living creatures like mosquitoes act as 'vectors' that carry parasites or viruses from one person to another. Easy peasy! [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h3)

question: Through which main exit route do tuberculosis (TB) germs travel when someone coughs into the air?
explanation: Since TB loves the lungs, coughing sends those tiny droplets flying right out through the respiratory tract into the air. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h4)

question: A nurse accidentally gets poked by a used needle. Which natural body defense was bypassed?
explanation: Your unbroken skin is an amazing armor against germs! A sharp needle poke breaks right through that armor and lets germs straight into the tissue. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which group of people usually has the highest risk of catching infections easily?
explanation: Babies are still building their immune defenses, and older adults have immune systems that slow down with age. Both groups need extra protection! [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why does severe lack of proper nutrition (malnutrition) make a patient much more likely to catch infections?

options.A: It alters the pH of the skin, making it too alkaline for pathogens
options.B: It impairs the body's ability to produce antibodies and white blood cells
options.C: It directly creates environmental reservoirs inside the gastrointestinal tract
options.D: it expands the portal of entry size for airborne microorganisms

explanation: Good food fuels your immune system! Without enough nutrients, the body struggles to build the white blood cells and antibodies needed to fight back. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h5)

question: During which early stage of an infection do vague, mild signs like tiredness first start to show?
explanation: The prodromal phase is that sneaky early stage where you just feel 'off' or unusually tired before the full-blown symptoms hit. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why is it so easy for germs to spread during the early prodromal stage?

options.A: The host has already developed complete immunity against the infectious agent
options.B: Patients feel well enough to move around and spread germs despite mild, vague symptoms
options.C: Pathogens are completely dormant and cannot trigger any immune response yet
options.D: Symptoms are so severe that patients refuse to leave isolation wards

explanation: Because people only feel a bit tired or slightly unwell, they keep going about their day—unwittingly sharing their germs everywhere they go! [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the single most important thing a nurse can do to stop the spread of hospital-acquired infections?
explanation: Simple, thorough handwashing is your absolute superpower in nursing. It washes away those hitchhiking germs instantly! [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h7)

question: A nurse wears sterile gloves and a face mask to put in a urinary catheter. Which link in the infection chain is mainly being blocked?
explanation: Sterile technique acts like a bouncer, making sure germs cannot sneak through the door into the clean urinary tract during the procedure. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h7)
